notes.meaning: The woman's husband questions why she is visiting Elisha on a regular working day. People in Israel often visited the prophets on holy days like the New Moon and Sabbath to hear God's word. She replies that everything is all right, keeping the boy's death quiet so she can reach the prophet without delay.

She prepares the donkey quickly and orders her servant to keep up a brisk pace. In Bible times, a servant walked or ran alongside to urge the animal forward. Her command shows great urgency and focused determination to get help.

She travels about fifteen miles to Mount Carmel, where Elisha spent time in prayer and teaching. Elisha spots her while she is still far off and recognizes her right away. He sends his servant Gehazi to meet her, showing his caring attention for his friends.

Gehazi runs forward to ask if she, her husband, and her child are well. She briefly replies that everything is well, saving her full sorrow for Elisha himself. Her answer also shows quiet faith that God will do what is right, even in the middle of heartbreak.

When she reaches Elisha on the hill, she falls down and grasps his feet in deep sorrow and pleading. Gehazi tries to push her away, but Elisha protects her and recognizes her deep pain. Elisha notes that the Lord did not reveal her trouble to him, proving that prophets only know what God chooses to show them.

The grieving mother reminds Elisha that she never asked for a child in the first place. She had begged him earlier not to give her false hopes by promising a son only to lose him. Her cry expresses her deep heartbreak while pleading for Elisha to make things right.

Elisha tells Gehazi to tuck his robe into his belt so he can run fast without stopping. He warns him not to waste time on long, formal greetings along the road, but to lay Elisha's staff on the child's face. The staff represented the prophet's authority, and the urgent mission required total focus.

The mother takes a solemn oath that she will not return home without Elisha himself. She put no confidence in a wooden staff or a servant, but insisted on the prophet's personal presence. Moved by her persistent faith and sorrow, Elisha gets up and follows her.

Gehazi goes ahead and places the staff on the child's face, but the boy makes no sound or movement. He goes back to Elisha to report that the boy has not awakened from death. This outcome showed that God's power does not work like a magic charm through an object, but requires prayer and direct divine intervention.

Elisha arrives at the house and climbs up to the guest room built for him. There he finds the boy lying dead upon his own bed, just as the mother had left him. The prophet now faces the full reality of the family's loss.

Elisha shuts the door so that only he and the dead body are in the room, keeping out noisy distractions and curious onlookers. He then turns directly to the Lord in fervent prayer. He knew that only God has the power to call the dead back to life.

Elisha lies down on the child, placing his mouth, eyes, and hands directly against the boy's body. Touching a dead body brought ceremonial defilement under the law, but doing an act of divine mercy took higher priority. As Elisha stretches out in prayer, the child's cold flesh begins to grow warm with returning life.

Elisha steps away and paces back and forth across the room, continuing to pray with deep earnestness. He stretches over the boy a second time, and the child sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. God brought the boy back to life step by step, showing how persistent prayer is rewarded.

Elisha calls Gehazi and tells him to bring the Shunammite mother into the room. When she arrives at the doorway, Elisha simply tells her to take up her living son. God had answered their cries and restored the boy to her loving care.

The mother falls at Elisha's feet and bows to the ground in humble thanks to God. She then picks up her living boy in her arms and leaves the room. Her deep grief was turned into overwhelming joy by God's kindness and power.

Elisha travels to Gilgal, where a school of the prophets was gathered during a severe famine. While the young prophets sit before him to receive his teaching, Elisha looks out for their physical needs as well. He instructs his servant to put on a large cooking pot and boil a stew for the hungry group.

One of the students goes out into the fields to gather wild plants for the meal. He comes across a wild climbing vine and fills his folded garment with wild gourds, likely poisonous colocynth melons. He cuts them up into the stew without knowing they are toxic and dangerous to eat.

The men begin to eat the stew, but the terrible bitter taste quickly warns them of danger. They cry out to Elisha that there is death in the pot, terrified that they have swallowed deadly poison. No one can finish the meal, and their only food appears ruined.

Elisha asks for a handful of flour and throws it into the bubbling pot. The flour had no natural medical power to cure poison, but God used it as an outward sign of His cleansing power. The stew becomes completely wholesome and safe for everyone to eat.

A generous man brings Elisha a gift of twenty barley loaves and freshly harvested grain. Under God's law, these first gathered crops usually went to the temple priests, but pious Israelites brought them to the prophets because the kingdom's religious worship was corrupt. Elisha does not keep the gift for himself, but orders it to be set out for the hungry men.

The servant wonders aloud how twenty small loaves could ever feed a crowd of one hundred men. Elisha repeats his order and declares God's promise that they will eat and still have leftovers. God's word assured them that His miraculous blessing would supply far more than their natural resources.

The servant serves the bread, and the hundred men eat until everyone is full, leaving bread behind just as the Lord promised. The bread multiplied as they ate by God's divine power. This miracle points forward to Jesus miraculously feeding thousands in the wilderness with just a few loaves.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some older critical scholars denied any miraculous multiplication, suggesting the men were simply satisfied with small portions or that the food was already sufficient.
